tldr: By temporarily ignoring complex walking dynamics to learn global navigation on a simplified reduced-order model (point-mass) and then transferring this knowledge to a humanoid, this paper achieves mapless multi-floor navigation—including stairs—on real hardware.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed "RoM-Nav" from training to real-world deployment. Using procedurally generated multi-story buildings in simulation, policies are transferred in stages from a simple cylinder model to the humanoid. On real hardware (Unitree G1), it autonomously navigates multi-floor environments without a map, tackling over 10 m of vertical displacement and more than 100 m of total path length.
overview:
Humanoid locomotion has advanced rapidly, allowing robots to walk across stairs and rough terrain with ease. However, when asked to autonomously navigate—like "go to that room on the upper floor"—the task becomes dramatically harder. Standard single-stage reinforcement learning (RL) that tries to learn navigation and locomotion all at once often fails. The robot frequently falls on stairs or gets stuck during exploration, causing training to collapse on long-distance tasks involving vertical (z-axis) movement across floors.

To address this, the authors cleanly separated "stepping through difficult terrain" from "moving intelligently through space." First, they treat the robot as a simple moving point mass (reduced-order model, or RoM) and quickly train a global navigation policy using only 3D LiDAR geometry across multiple floors. Next, this RoM policy acts as a teacher to kickstart training on the full-order humanoid dynamics, blending imitation and reinforcement learning while keeping the locomotion controller frozen.

Furthermore, for real-world deployment, they incorporate an online "Poisson safety filter" that corrects velocities in real time to avoid out-of-distribution (OOD) obstacles never seen during training.

Experiments show a substantial boost in cross-floor navigation success rates compared to single-stage RL, while halving the fall rate on stairs. On a real Unitree G1 robot without any prior map, the framework achieved fully autonomous navigation across outdoor terrains and multi-story buildings, covering vertical climbs over 10 m and total travel distances exceeding 100 m.
contributions: First demonstration of mapless, cross-floor autonomous navigation across multiple building levels on a physical humanoid robot
A two-stage kickstarting pipeline that first learns global navigation on a reduced-order model (point-mass) and then distills and transfers it to the full-order humanoid
Zero collisions against out-of-distribution obstacles achieved via an online Poisson safety filter, without sacrificing navigation success rate

sections.heading: The Challenge of Multi-Level Navigation: Why Is Humanoid Navigation So Hard?
sections.summary: Humanoid locomotion is advancing, but navigating complex multi-level environments with stairs remains exceptionally difficult. Standard single-stage RL suffers from exploration collapse, prompting the authors to propose a two-stage reduced-order learning approach with a safety filter.
sections.details:
Humanoid locomotion has achieved remarkable progress, demonstrating stair climbing and even parkour. However, putting these agile walking skills to work for autonomous building navigation is a completely different challenge. The high-level navigation plan is tightly coupled with whether the locomotion controller can safely traverse the ground underfoot.

Reinforcement learning (RL) allows generating commands directly from raw sensor observations, bypassing heavy real-time optimization or occupancy grid mapping. Yet in long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards (where a reward is received only upon reaching the goal), misstepping on stairs leads to frequent falls, causing exploration to break down.

To solve this, the authors introduce a two-stage learning pipeline. First, they train a navigation policy from LiDAR observations on a reduced-order model (RoM) that ignores complex foot-terrain interactions. Using action distributions from this RoM policy as hints (kickstarting), they then fine-tune on the full humanoid dynamics with a frozen locomotion controller. This significantly outperforms conventional single-stage learning, especially on multi-story tasks requiring vertical (z-axis) spatial reasoning.

Finally, to avoid collisions with unknown real-world obstacles, an online Poisson safety filter constructs a control barrier function (CBF) directly from LiDAR point clouds to guarantee execution safety.

sections.heading: What Sets This Apart: Leaping from 2D Planes to 3D Multi-Story Space
sections.summary: Prior learning-based navigation on quadrupeds and humanoids has almost exclusively focused on single-floor 2D planar movement. This work expands into multi-story 3D navigation by combining low-fidelity kickstarting with a model-free safety filter.
sections.details:
Humanoid navigation has traditionally relied on model-based methods, convex region optimization, and dense environmental maps (SLAM). While recent sensor-to-action learning methods have emerged, they have been restricted to short-range obstacle avoidance or tracking predefined waypoints.

Meanwhile, RL navigation has been extensively studied on quadrupeds. However, existing training setups have focused strictly on single-floor planar environments. In those setups, stairs and ramps are treated merely as obstacles to overcome along the way. Situations where the goal's elevation (z-coordinate) carries critical meaning independent of planar coordinates have not been addressed.

Training navigation on low-fidelity models (point-mass or kinematic models) before deploying to real robots has been explored previously, but only for zero-shot transfer in flat environments. As shown in this paper, relying solely on low-fidelity models in environments with stairs and steep slopes leads to falls. Thus, a second training stage accounting for the humanoid's full-order dynamics is essential.

Moreover, unlike existing runtime safety methods that rely on learned value functions or object detectors, this approach uniquely derives a barrier function directly from raw point clouds using a Poisson safety filter.

captions.F2: Network architecture and training pipeline of RoM-Nav. Features from LiDAR and depth images are extracted using a pre-trained CNN, then processed through Attention and GRU modules to output velocity commands. As shown in the bottom diagram, global exploration is first learned on a simple reduced-order model (RoM), and this knowledge is then transferred to the full humanoid via a KL-divergence kickstart loss.

sections.heading: How RoM-Nav Works: Combining Reduced-Order Pre-training and a Safety Filter
sections.summary: The method is built on four core pillars: a pre-trained LiDAR encoder, kickstarting from a reduced-order model, procedural multi-story terrain generation with tailored sampling, and an online Poisson safety filter.
sections.details:
The approach targets the Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with a head-mounted Livox Mid-360 LiDAR and a ZED Mini depth camera. The locomotion controller uses LIP-CLF RL, kept frozen while the high-level navigation policy runs at 5 Hz.

### III-A Pre-training the Vision Encoder
To reliably extract features from LiDAR range and depth images, a variational autoencoder (VAE) is pre-trained, and its encoder is frozen. In addition to reconstructing depth and 3D coordinates, it is trained on semantic segmentation of stairs, slopes, ground, and obstacles. This ensures that critical terrain features for navigation are preserved in the latent space.

### III-B Policy Architecture
The observation space includes the encoded LiDAR and depth features, alongside non-visual inputs such as relative goal position $o_g$, previous actions, and gait phase. These are fused via Self-Attention and Cross-Attention and fed into a 2-layer GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit), giving the policy memory under partial observability. The action output specifies forward, lateral, and yaw velocities modeled via Beta distributions.

### III-C Kickstarting with a Reduced-Order Model (RoM)
The robot is first modeled as a planar point-mass system (a first-order integrator with translation and yaw) and trained for 2,000 PPO iterations in the RoM environment. Next, training moves to the full humanoid environment for another 2,000 iterations, adding a KL-divergence loss against the RoM policy to the standard PPO objective (with weight $\lambda$ initialized at 1.0 and decayed to 0.05). Total compute time is under 45 hours on a single H100 GPU.

### III-D RL Environment and Sampling Design
To simulate multi-story structures, procedural tiles are generated where multiple distinct floors share the same $(x, y)$ coordinates. To promote stair traversal, robots have a 30% reset probability of being placed at the base of stairs or ramps, initialized with poses drawn from a locomotion library. Goal sampling is capped at a 30 m geodesic distance (accounting for walls), with a 100% bias toward placing goals on different floors in multi-story tiles.

### III-E Poisson Safety Filter
To handle out-of-distribution obstacles, a 2D occupancy grid is built from LiDAR points, and a smooth safety function $h(p)$ is computed in real time by solving Poisson's equation. For a desired velocity $v_{\text{des}}$ output by the policy, a quadratic program (QP) finds the closest velocity satisfying the control barrier function (CBF) condition $\dot{h} \ge -\alpha h$ and sends it to the locomotion controller.

captions.F3: Examples of environment tiles and occupancy grids used in training. (a)(b) show a 3-story building tile and its per-floor occupancy grids, while (c)(d) show outdoor tiles with elevation changes. Because multi-story structures share identical planar coordinates across different floors, consistent floor-specific maps are maintained for training the reduced-order model.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Decisive Advantage on Cross-Floor Tasks and Real-World Stair Climbing
sections.summary: In simulation, the proposed method substantially outperforms single-stage learning on cross-floor navigation. Real-world experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the Poisson safety filter against OOD obstacles and show successful autonomous navigation over 10 m of elevation gain and 100 m of distance.
sections.details:
### IV-A Effect of RoM Kickstarting
Evaluated across 1,024 initial conditions in simulation, the single-stage baseline trained directly on the humanoid achieved only a 66.5% success rate within 120 seconds. In contrast, the proposed RoM-Nav reached 88.2%, approaching the theoretical upper bound of the reduced-order model alone (89.8%).
Looking closer, both methods performed similarly on same-floor tasks, but RoM-Nav held a massive advantage on cross-level tasks involving stairs. Deploying the RoM policy directly resulted in a 16.3% fall rate on stairs, whereas kickstarting cut this fall rate roughly in half to 8.3%.

### IV-B Ablation Studies
Removing the pre-trained LiDAR encoder and learning it from scratch with PPO severely degraded success rates. Similarly, removing stair-proximal resets or geodesic distance limits sharply lowered cross-floor success, validating the importance of each design choice.

### IV-C Safety Against Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Obstacles
In hardware tests, the authors introduced stepladders, protruding cardboard tubes, and suspended thin pipes—adversarial obstacles with minimal LiDAR cross-sections. Without the CBF safety filter, the robot collided with the thin pipe 4 times and the stepladder twice. With CBF enabled, it achieved zero collisions across all 10 trials.

### IV-D Long-Range Multi-Story Real-World Deployment
Using the physical Unitree G1, experiments were conducted across four challenging real-world environments. Exceeding the maximum training parameters (8 m vertical, 30 m distance), the robot successfully navigated a 10 m vertical climb across two floors and an outdoor course exceeding 100 m with stairs and rough ground—all mapless, fully autonomous, and without a single collision or fall.

captions.F5: Trajectory comparisons with and without the safety filter (CBF) on out-of-distribution (OOD) obstacles. Both perform similarly on standard in-distribution obstacles (left). For the stepladder (middle) and suspended thin pipe (right), navigating without CBF (red) causes collisions (marked with 'x'), whereas enabling CBF (blue) cleanly avoids them and reaches the goal.
captions.F6: Real-world autonomous navigation examples on the Unitree G1. The robot conquered a cluttered lab (top-left, 38 m), a two-floor open-atrium staircase with wire railings (top-right, 51 m, 7 m vertical rise), an outdoor-to-indoor two-floor staircase climb (bottom-left, 51 m, 10 m vertical rise), and a long outdoor path (bottom-right, 100 m), all fully autonomously.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Toward Full-Body Safety and Real-World Navigation
sections.summary: Kickstarting from a reduced-order model combined with a Poisson safety filter enabled mapless multi-story autonomous navigation on a humanoid. Future challenges include detecting transparent objects and ensuring full-body safety.
sections.details:
This paper presents RoM-Nav, a framework enabling mapless autonomous multi-floor navigation on humanoid robots. By first training global navigation on a reduced-order model isolated from complex foot-terrain interactions, and then kickstarting the full humanoid policy, the approach proves highly effective for tasks requiring vertical spatial exploration.

At the same time, clear challenges remain for real-world deployment. LiDAR cannot detect glass walls or transparent automatic doors, requiring cardboard coverings on certain windows during experiments. Additionally, the approach assumes an accurate relative 3D goal vector in the robot's local frame. The 2D planar assumption in the safety filter could also theoretically block viable paths (though this was not observed in experiments). Addressing these limitations and extending toward full-body safety guarantees will be exciting directions for future research.

takeaways: Even with complex humanoid dynamics, a divide-and-conquer strategy—learning global navigation on a simple point-mass model (RoM) first and then kickstarting knowledge transfer—is remarkably effective.
For multi-floor 3D navigation, specialized sampling designs such as stair-proximal resets and geodesic distance constraints are critical to training success.
Filtering RL policy outputs in real time through a control barrier function (Poisson safety filter) eliminates collisions with out-of-distribution obstacles without degrading navigation performance.
limitations: Relying solely on LiDAR means glass doors and transparent walls cannot be detected, requiring manual workarounds such as taping cardboard over glass during trials.
Relies on the strong assumption that an accurate 3D relative goal position in the robot's frame is known at all times.
Because the safety filter relies on a 2D planar projection, it may struggle to distinguish small obstacles the robot can step over from head-height overhangs.
